title: Silver Has Crashed 53% From Its January Peak and Gold Is Down 26%: What Broke the Rally
excerpt: Silver fell from about $117-$121 an ounce in January to around $54 by October 23, while gold dropped 26% from its January record — a reversal driven by rate-hike expectations, higher energy prices and margin-driven selling.
body:
• Silver has fallen more than 53% from its January 2026 record — from a peak near $117-$121 an ounce to around $54 by October 23 — while gold has dropped 26% from its all-time January peak.
  • In India, MCX silver fell from a record Rs 4,20,048 per kg in January to about Rs 1,92,800-Rs 1,95,500 per kg in late October.
  • The reversal is blamed on rising energy prices, the West Asia crisis and persistent inflation strengthening expectations of further US rate hikes — the opposite of the usual safe-haven pattern.
  • Analysts cited in market coverage see $50 as crucial silver support and a possible recovery toward $90-$100 by next Dhanteras if geopolitical pressure eases — a forecast, not a guarantee.

The precious-metals rally of early 2026 has unwound violently. Silver prices fell more than 53% from their January record as Middle East tensions and persistent inflation weighed on bullion, with silver peaking near $117 per ounce in late January before falling to around $54 by October 23, and gold dropping 26% from its all-time peak in January, according to Inshorts. Spot gold had surged to $5,419 an ounce in January.

Silver's fall is roughly double gold's, and the reason is structural. About half of silver demand is industrial — solar panels, electronics and manufacturing — so when higher energy costs and inflation raise the prospect of further Federal Reserve rate hikes, silver is hit as both a monetary and an industrial metal. Gold, bought heavily by central banks, has a floor silver lacks.

The India numbers

Domestic prices tell the same story in rupees. MCX silver futures hit a record high of Rs 4.20 lakh per kg in January 2026 and fell to Rs 1,94,170 per kg on October 23; December-delivery futures traded at Rs 1,95,500 per kg on Monday, October 26 — a decline of approximately 54 per cent from the January peak, according to 7Globe's market coverage. International prices corrected about 56% from $121.64 to $53.47 on the measures cited there — small differences between reports reflect spot versus futures benchmarks, not disagreement about the scale of the crash.

"We believe this correction offers gradual accumulation opportunities, with $50 providing crucial support. As geopolitical pressures ease, silver could potentially recover towards $90-100 by next Dhanteras, although volatility may persist."

— Analyst commentary cited by 7Globe

Why the safe haven failed

The unusual feature of 2026 is that war raised oil instead of bullion. With Brent crude trading above $110 in the accounts cited, rising inflation risks increased expectations of Fed rate hikes, pressuring non-yielding metals, while weakness in equity markets pointed to liquidity pressure rather than a flight to safety. Leveraged futures positions amplified the fall: exchanges raising margin requirements force holders to sell, whatever their view of the metal.

For diaspora buyers, the timing is painful in a specific way. January's peak coincided with peak wedding-season and investment buying, and Diwali purchases made near the highs are deeply underwater. The analyst case for accumulation rests on silver's structural deficit and industrial demand — but the same coverage is explicit that volatility may persist, and a 53% drawdown is a reminder that silver is not a savings account. Anyone averaging down is making a market bet, not recovering a deposit.
